causalMechanism.primaryVector: Traumatic brain injury disrupts the peripheral vestibular system through mechanical and vascular injury. Impact forces transmitted to the temporal bone and labyrinth produce labyrinthine concussion with damage to the membranous labyrinth and sensory epithelia; acceleration-deceleration of the head shears the otolithic membrane and dislodges otoconia from the utricle, which migrate into a semicircular canal (most often the posterior canal) and cause positionally triggered endolymph flow — the canalithiasis mechanism of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI, the onset and pattern of positional vertigo or imbalance relative to the injury, and objective vestibular findings (positive Dix-Hallpike or supine roll maneuver with characteristic nystagmus for BPPV; videonystagmography, video head impulse, caloric, or vestibular-evoked myogenic potential testing for non-positional deficits), and address competing causes — pre-existing or idiopathic BPPV (common in the general population, so temporal proximity to trauma is essential), vestibular migraine, Meniere's disease, medication ototoxicity, and central or cerebellar causes. causalMechanism.primaryVector: Traumatic brain injury causes hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction through several converging mechanisms. Direct mechanical forces can fracture the skull base and sella, shear the pituitary stalk, and injure the median eminence, while rotational acceleration damages the fine hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal vasculature and the pituitary itself. Subsequent edema, hemorrhage, and hypoxic-ischemic injury (from apnea, hypotension, or raised intracranial pressure) further compromise the hypothalamic neurons and pituitary secretory cells that regulate the axes. The result is deficient synthesis or release of one or more anterior pituitary hormones: growth hormone (most commonly), gonadotropins leading to hypogonadism, thyrotropin leading to central hypothyroidism, corticotropin leading to secondary adrenal insufficiency, and less commonly antidiuretic hormone deficiency. Early post-injury abnormalities may be transient, but a substantial proportion of patients develop persistent deficits that are detectable at 12 months or later, and untreated deficiency produces fatigue, impaired quality of life, adverse metabolic profiles, and impaired recovery. The evidence base is quantitative and consistent: a systematic review pooling 19 studies of 1,137 patients found chronic-phase hypopituitarism in 27.5% (95% CI 22.8-28.9) after TBI, with higher prevalence after severe TBI; a meta-analysis of 29 studies and 2,756 participants found at least one anterior pituitary hormone dysfunction in 32% (95% CI 25-38) at 12 months or more (34% in high-quality studies); and a 2024 meta-analysis of 52 studies and 7,367 participants found any pituitary axis dysfunction in 33% (95% CI 28-37), with growth hormone deficiency 18%, gonadal deficiency 16%, ACTH deficiency 10%, and TSH deficiency 6%, and multiple affected axes in 7%. Legally, 38 CFR § 3.310(d)(1)(v) provides that diseases of hormone deficiency that result from hypothalamo-pituitary changes are presumed to be the proximate result of a service-connected TBI when they manifest within 12 months of moderate or severe TBI; where that presumption does not apply (mild TBI, or manifestation outside 12 months), § 3.310(d)(2) directs decision under generally applicable principles, i.e., a § 3.310(a) causation opinion. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity using the § 3.310(d)(3) criteria (loss of consciousness, alteration of consciousness, post-traumatic amnesia, Glasgow Coma Scale, imaging), the date of manifestation of the hormone deficiency relative to the injury, and endocrinologic testing of the affected axes (morning cortisol with stimulation testing where indicated, IGF-1, LH/FSH with testosterone or estradiol, TSH with free T4, prolactin, and sodium/osmolality for diabetes insipidus), and exclude competing causes — pituitary adenoma or other sellar mass, cranial radiotherapy, hypophysitis, Sheehan's syndrome, hemochromatosis, infiltrative disease, and drug effects.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Traumatic brain injury produces epilepsy through a well-characterized epileptogenic cascade. Focal cortical contusion, subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhage, and shearing of white-matter tracts create a structural lesion with hemosiderin deposition, blood-brain-barrier disruption, and reactive gliosis; injured neurons and glia release glutamate and inflammatory mediators that produce excitotoxic injury, while loss of inhibitory interneurons and aberrant axonal sprouting (mossy fiber reorganization) establish a hyperexcitable network capable of spontaneous seizure generation. The latent period between injury and the first unprovoked seizure reflects this progressive epileptogenesis, and lesional features visible on imaging (cortical contusion, subdural hematoma) are among the most consistently reported risk factors. The epidemiological evidence is strong and severity-dependent: a population-based cohort of 4,541 patients with TBI (Olmsted County, 1935-1984) found an overall standardized incidence ratio of 3.1 (95% CI 2.5-3.8), with SIR 1.5 after mild injury (no increase beyond five years), 2.9 after moderate injury, and 17.0 after severe injury; a Danish population-based cohort of 1,605,216 people found relative risks of 2.22 (95% CI 2.07-2.38) after mild injury, 7.40 (6.16-8.89) after severe injury, and 2.17 (1.73-2.71) after skull fracture, with risk still elevated more than 10 years later (severe injury RR 4.29, 95% CI 2.04-9.00) and especially high in those injured after age 15 (severe injury RR 12.24, 95% CI 8.52-17.57); and a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies (242,803 patients) found a pooled post-traumatic seizure incidence of 7.2% (95% CI 5.4-9.3), with severe TBI, subdural hematoma, cortical contusions, and older age the most consistently reported risk factors in individual studies. Legally, 38 CFR § 3.310(d)(1)(ii) provides that unprovoked seizures following moderate or severe TBI are held to be the proximate result of the service-connected TBI absent clear evidence to the contrary; where the injury was mild or the claim falls outside the presumption, § 3.310(d)(2) routes the claim to generally applicable principles and a § 3.310(a) opinion. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity using the § 3.310(d)(3) criteria, the imaging findings (contusion, hemorrhage, encephalomalacia), the seizure semiology with a witness account and the date of first unprovoked seizure relative to the injury, and the electroencephalographic and neurologic workup; exclude competing causes — pre-existing epilepsy, alcohol withdrawal, metabolic derangements, medication or drug effects, central nervous system infection, tumor, and syncope or non-epileptic events misclassified as seizures. Where seizures predate the injury, only attributable worsening is service-connected under § 3.310(b).

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Traumatic brain injury produces chronic insomnia through structural and functional injury to the sleep-wake regulatory system rather than through pain or psychological factors alone. The ascending arousal system (brainstem cholinergic and monoaminergic nuclei), the hypothalamic sleep-wake switch including orexin/hypocretin neurons, the suprachiasmatic nucleus and its light-entrainment input, and the thalamocortical circuits that generate sleep spindles are all vulnerable to shearing, contusion, and hypoxic-ischemic injury; diffuse axonal injury and neuroinflammation (microglial activation with cytokine release, including interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor) further disturb sleep homeostasis and circadian timing. Clinically this produces sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance insomnia, fragmentation, and non-restorative sleep, often with excessive daytime sleepiness, and the disturbance can persist for years after the injury and impede rehabilitation. The epidemiologic evidence is substantial: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies (19 meta-analyzed, n = 95,195) found pooled prevalence of post-mild-TBI insomnia disorder of 27.0% (95% CI 6.49-54.68) and insomnia symptoms of 71.7% (95% CI 60.31-81.85), significantly higher than general-population estimates, though heterogeneity was high; a second, larger synthesis of 69 studies found adults with prior mild TBI reported worse subjective sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index elevations) at every recovery phase from under a week to one year and beyond, while objective sleep-stage differences were less robust after bias adjustment; and a mechanistic review documents the neural-network, neuroendocrine, sleep-wake-regulator, and immune-inflammatory pathways implicated in post-TBI sleep-wake disturbance. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a chronic insomnia disorder developing after a service-connected TBI is a direct-causation secondary claim; insomnia is not among the conditions listed in § 3.310(d)(1), so an individual medical opinion is required. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity using the § 3.310(d)(3) criteria, the sleep history with onset relative to the injury and persistence over time (sleep diary, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index or insomnia severity measures, and polysomnography where indicated), and the treatment history; exclude or account for competing causes — obstructive and central sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements, circadian rhythm disorders, pain, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and depression, substance and medication effects (including stimulants and sedatives), and primary insomnia predating the injury.
